schools.summary: Henry rests the claim on the precept rather than merit, and turns it into a standing rule that those who preach the gospel should live of it.
Gill sets the moment after the tribal division and the cities of refuge; Calvin judges the delay disgraceful to Israel, who needed reminding of a plain command.
Clarke lays out the three Levite families and the warrant of Numbers 35; Wesley names the heads then living.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the family structure of Levi that governs the whole distribution.
Gill fixes the place at Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood and the lot was being cast.
Wesley reads 'the Lord commanded' as binding beyond its occasion.
Gill notes Israel raised no objection and gave freely out of inheritances just received.
Clarke reads cheerful obedience and the lot as divine designation; Wesley argues the Levites held absolute dominion of the suburbs, not merely their use.
Keil and Delitzsch tabulate the four allotments and quote Calvin on the priests' placing.
Gill marks the first lot; Calvin denies it was chance and meets the objection that Jerusalem was not given them.
Clarke explains the larger share by the rule of Numbers 35:8; Wesley reads the grant as made for future generations.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the tally of ten towns from Ephraim, Dan and half Manasseh.
Gill defines 'the rest' by descent through Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel.
Clarke argues at length that the Levites held houses and pasture rather than the towns entire, and were never confined to them.
Keil and Delitzsch answer the objection of scale with the size of the towns, the terms of the grant, and the census figure.
Gill notes the Gershonite cities lay in the more distant tribes.
Keil and Delitzsch defend the number of towns and raise the harder objection about the priests' thirteen.
Gill identifies Merari's descendants without further comment.
Keil and Delitzsch flag the independent and defective parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6.
Gill reads the dispersion as fulfilling Jacob's word and as a benefit to the tribes.
Keil and Delitzsch structure the priestly section and protect Caleb's fields.
Henry argues the Levites held their towns as proprietors, and draws four observations from the shape of the list.
Gill marks the transition into the roll of names.
Wesley explains why Judah and Simeon are named together.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the doubled grant of Hebron as resumption after the parenthesis about Caleb, and prefer Ashan to Ain.
Gill supplies the priestly descent through Aaron.
Wesley notes the plural 'families' standing for the singular.
Keil and Delitzsch take the verse at face value.
Gill reports Kimchi's reading of Anak as a general name for the giants, with Arba their chief.
Clarke refers the identification back to Joshua 14:15.

themes: Hebron at the head of the list

schools.summary: Gill defines the excluded portion as what lay beyond the two thousand cubits.
Clarke reads it as an exclusive privilege untouched by the Levitical grant; Wesley extends the case to every city in the chapter and finds a persuasive purpose in recording it.

themes: a rule for the whole list

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch had marked this verse as the resumption of the interrupted grant.
Gill identifies the recipients as the priestly line within Kohath.

fidelity.note: K&D's explanation of the resumption sits under verse 10; applied here because their block spans vv.10-13.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch carry the identifications forward and record where a town is absent from the tribal allotment.
Gill refers each name to his earlier treatment.

themes: nine towns from Judah and Simeon
Anathoth and Almon missing from Benjamin's list

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place Holon among the hill-country towns of Joshua 15:51.
Gill sends the reader to his earlier note on the town.
Gill refers to his earlier treatment of the name.
Wesley notes Ain and Gibeon are missing from 1 Chronicles 6:59 and offers destruction or a change of name as alternatives.
Keil and Delitzsch identify both towns from Benjamin's allotment.
Gill connects the town to the Gibeonites of Joshua 9.
Keil and Delitzsch close the priestly total and open the Kohathite section with its identifications.
Gill assembles Jerome, Rauwolff and Josephus on the site and notes its absence from Benjamin's own catalogue.
Clarke agrees on the distance from Jerusalem on Jerome's authority.
Gill identifies the recipients once more.
Clarke answers the objection of scale by the priests' later increase into the courses of David's day.
Calvin explains the dispersion as a punishment on Levi converted into the highest honour, the Levites made guardians of pure worship in every district; Gill identifies the recipients.
Wesley glosses 'which remained' as those over and above the priests.

themes: dispersion as punishment turned to honour

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch run the identifications through Ephraim, Dan and Manasseh, and do extended philological work on Beeshterah while refusing the identification with Busra.
Gill locates Shechem in Mount Ephraim.

themes: Beeshterah and the house of Astarte

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch propose Jockmeam of 1 Chronicles 6:68 as a possible equivalent, itself undiscovered.
Gill suggests Kibzaim may be Jokneam but concedes the name occurs nowhere else.
Clarke notes there were two cities called Beth-horon and which is meant cannot be ascertained.
Keil and Delitzsch place both towns in Dan's allotment at Joshua 19:44.
Gill refers the name to his earlier treatment.
Keil and Delitzsch identify both towns from Dan's allotment.
Gill refers to his earlier note.
Clarke points back to the valley of Aijalon in Joshua 10:12.

themes: a name repeated in the list

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch place Taanach among Manasseh's towns; the repeated Gath-rimmon belongs with the section's other irregularities.
Gill refers the names to his earlier treatment.
Gill breaks the ten down as four from Ephraim, four from Dan and two from half Manasseh.
Keil and Delitzsch expand Beeshterah as Beth-eshterah, weigh Eusebius and Jerome as too indefinite, and exclude Busra outright.
Gill identifies the Gershonites by descent.
Clarke refers the cities of refuge to his fuller discussion at Joshua 20:7.
Keil and Delitzsch identify the four towns and continue into Asher and Naphtali, judging Hukok for Helkath a copyist's error.
Gill connects the town and the river and reports its alternative names.

Keil and Delitzsch place both towns in Asher's allotment.

Keil and Delitzsch identify Jokneam and Nahalal and record Kartah and Dimnah as unknown.

Clarke refers Jahazah to his earlier note at Joshua 13:18.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the closing paragraph as the conclusion of the whole division from Joshua 13 onward, joining the book's two halves.
Gill traces Heshbon from Sihon's royal city to Reuben and then to Gad.

Gill sums the four sections; Calvin infers from the figure that many cities of the other tribes went unmentioned, since Levi was the least numerous tribe.

themes: unnamed cities of the other tribes

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch had glossed the repeated noun as meaning city by city.
Gill takes the suburbs at their legal measure and purpose.

fidelity.note: K&D's gloss on the distributive 'city city' sits under verse 37; applied here as their block spans the summary.

schools.summary: Henry sets performance against promise so that each illuminates the other, and draws the parallel to the heavenly Canaan.

Gill distinguishes the grant by lot from actual occupation and attributes the remainder to Israel's sloth and to God's own design of gradual dispossession; Calvin resolves the difficulty by distinguishing God's steadfast faithfulness from the people's voluntary torpor.
Clarke argues tribute proves subjugation and insists the promise was always conditional on obedience.
Keil and Delitzsch trace the wording to Deuteronomy 12:9 and explain the surviving Canaanites as powerless while Israel was faithful.
Henry describes the rest in its parts and marks that it lasted until Israel put thorns into their own beds.
Gill defines the rest by the travels and wars it ended.
Wesley bounds the rest to the days of Joshua.
Keil and Delitzsch state the limit honestly: Israel never held the whole land to the boundaries of Numbers 34, never conquering Tyre and Sidon.
Henry hears a testimony subscribed by Israel and repeated by Solomon, and lays any apparent shortfall to Israel's own charge.
Gill reads the doubled phrasing as covering every particular of every good thing.
Wesley makes the same testimony the confession of all believers in Christ.
